Project debt matches repayment to lease cash flow, limits direct recourse to the parent, and allows development at a scale far beyond what the corporate balance sheet could support independently.

The building adds another layer, as owned greenfield, owned brownfield, build-to-suit, and colocation each trade cash intensity against cooling efficiency, control, and lease obligations in very different ways.

That combination makes a generic capex-per-megawatt assumption especially dangerous for Nebius, because the cost of a future megawatt depends on which hardware generation fills it and which physical structure houses it.

We remain bullish on $MELI while expecting operating margins to stay between 6% and 8% through 2028. Our new model gives MercadoLibre another two years of heavy spending before earnings begin to reflect the scale of the business being built. Investors waiting for a quick recovery in profitability could have a frustrating stretch ahead.

Revenue grew 49.8% to $10.2 billion in Q2, while operating margin fell from 12.2% to 6.7% year over year. We understand why that combination worries people. MercadoLibre is lowering shipping thresholds, offering seller incentives and expanding a lending business that consumes capital and exposes shareholders to credit losses. Calling all of that investment only gets you so far. Eventually, the customers acquired through that spending have to generate enough profit to justify it.

Our new 2030 model and report are now live. We worked through commerce, advertising, payments, logistics and the lending portfolio to estimate what those customers could earn for MercadoLibre and how much shareholders must contribute along the way.

In commerce, much of our forecast comes from people buying more frequently. Cheaper shipping makes smaller purchases worthwhile, more parcels improve delivery density, and greater shopping activity makes advertising more valuable to sellers. Our base case takes annual purchases per buyer from roughly 33 to 49 between 2025 and 2030. That requires MercadoLibre to win more of the routine purchases people still make elsewhere.

Credit cards take longer to pay off. A new account brings acquisition costs, rewards and expected-loss provisions before it has developed much borrowing history. Older accounts can become profitable while rapid issuance keeps the overall card business losing money. 

Our base case includes roughly $3.6 billion of cumulative direct card losses from 2026 through 2028, after funding costs, provisions, servicing, rewards and acquisition expenses. We expect direct card contribution to turn positive in 2029.

We are willing to carry those losses in a bullish forecast because we expect the accounts being added today to become substantially more profitable as they mature. That assumption needs close scrutiny. Cards reach 62% of the lending portfolio in our 2030 base case, so disappointing card economics would affect a large part of the business.

Funding matters too. As the loan book grows, MercadoLibre must cover the portion that external financing cannot support. Our model deducts that additional parent capital when calculating cash available to shareholders. We also keep the benefits of greater customer engagement inside the shopping and payment assumptions where they already contribute, avoiding an extra valuation premium for the same activity.

Our base case reaches approximately $115 billion of revenue, $12.6 billion of net income and $11.35 billion of normalized cash flow to equity in 2030. Operating margin reaches 15%, with much of the improvement arriving in 2029 and 2030 as card profitability improves and growth spending takes a smaller share of revenue. These are our estimates, and the timing depends on management eventually allowing more of that profit to reach the income statement.

Our bear case still reaches almost $93 billion of revenue. Weaker card economics and continued heavy spending hold operating margin at 9.5%, leaving net income below half our base forecast. MercadoLibre could keep gaining customers for years and deliver disappointing returns if those customers cost too much to serve.

We think the long-term opportunity is worth the wait and the risks, but we want readers to see exactly what we are assuming. The operating research, funding analysis and four scenarios are available publicly. The report is linked in the first reply. If you disagree with our assumptions about card profitability, shipping costs or when margins recover, the model lets you work through what your view would mean for the stock.

The demand for greater control over AI gives the company an opportunity to develop its own enterprise customer base while today’s hyperscaler contracts help finance the infrastructure.

For a bank running financial-crime models or a biotech company working with proprietary research, choosing an AI provider involves decisions about data, access, security and dependence on that supplier. 

Nebius already has British customers including Revolut, Basecamp Research and Prima Mente, alongside a £1.7 billion UK expansion programme expected to reach 65 MW across four sites in 2027. Its operating base in Finland and larger projects in Finland and France give that strategy room to grow.

We see European AI sovereignty as a meaningful commercial tailwind for Nebius. Government support for domestic AI companies can help finance the customers buying compute, while local infrastructure and stronger customer controls can make more enterprise workloads accessible. Winning that business would give Nebius a broader source of demand and direct relationships it can develop over years.

Jim, this is the same state-matching error as the connected-MW argument in our $NBIS model that we addressed, just moved from the operating model to the balance sheet.

Yes, our 2029 and 2030 revenue estimates are far above the Street. We think the Street is wrong.

Yes, our Base case deploys roughly $285B of cumulative growth CapEx through 2030.

We published that because the entire point of the model is to determine how much of Nebius’s operating growth survives depreciation, financing, leases, replacement capital and dilution.

But the 6% to 12% “ROIC” calculation does not match the numerator and denominator correctly.

First, the approximately $250B denominator is not our depreciated invested-capital base.

It is almost exactly the average of our cumulative gross growth-CapEx balances at the end of 2029 and 2030:

2029: $217.6B
2030: $285.0B
Average: ~$251.3B

That is a gross deployed-capital figure, not depreciated net operating capital.

Our Base model recognizes approximately $101.7B of cumulative GAAP D&A from 2026 through 2030.

You cannot subtract depreciation from the EBIT numerator while leaving the capital denominator essentially gross.

And if you are changing the depreciation schedule from five years to ten years while holding the $250B “depreciated capital base” constant, the calculation is internally inconsistent.

A longer life raises EBIT, but it also raises net PP&E.

A shorter life lowers EBIT, but it also lowers net PP&E.

You cannot change one side of the ROIC fraction and freeze the other.

The fact that the answer doubles from 6% to 12% solely because the accounting life changes is the first clue that this is primarily an accounting-depreciation output, not a clean measure of underlying cash economics.

Second, 2030 is still a massive construction year, not a stabilized terminal year.

Our Base case spends approximately $67.4B of growth CapEx in 2030 alone and adds another 1.3GW of connected capacity.

Year-end billable IT capacity reaches approximately 5.136GW.

Average billable IT capacity during the year is only about 4.553GW.

That difference matters because the capital is already sitting in the denominator while a large portion of the corresponding capacity contributes only partial-year revenue.

Our 2030 Base case has:

AI-platform exit ARR: $116.7B
Recognized group revenue: $103.2B

That is a roughly $13.6B annualization gap on assets already substantially included in the year-end capital base.

At the modeled 54.4% EBITDA margin, annualizing the existing year-end run rate adds roughly $7.4B of operating earnings without adding another dollar to the capital denominator.

Using your same $250B gross denominator, annualizing the 2030 exit run rate and applying our actual seven-year economic replacement schedule produces roughly a 12% pretax operating return.

We do not need a ten-year life to get there.

If you want to use annual 2030 EBIT, the denominator should be average net invested capital during the year.

If you want to use the fully loaded year-end asset base, the numerator should be the annualized earnings capacity of that asset base.

Using partial-year earnings against fully loaded capital is the capital-side version of dividing annual recognized revenue by year-end connected MW.

Third, actual ROIC has to account for customer-funded operating capital.

Our Base case ends 2030 with approximately $60.5B of deferred revenue, largely created by customer prepayments.

Those prepayments are not free money, and we have never claimed they are.

But they are non-interest-bearing operating financing.

A proper invested-capital calculation cannot treat all of the corresponding assets as though Nebius funded them itself while ignoring the customer liability financing the build.

Management expects more than $9B of customer prepayments in 2026 alone.

Roughly 70% of Q2 deals included prepayments, covering 50% to 60% of associated CapEx.

So the roughly $250B gross-asset denominator is not merely inconsistent with depreciation.

It also fails to distinguish between capital funded by Nebius and capital supplied by customers through the operating cycle.

Fourth, the disclosed contract economics do not describe a 6% project-return business.

Nebius’s four major Q2 contracts averaged more than $1B of total contract value each and carried $20M to $25M of annual contract value per MW.

Management also disclosed:

70% of deals included prepayments

Those prepayments covered 50% to 60% of associated CapEx

Expected payback on associated CapEx and related operating costs was one year and ten months

Nebius could sell its entire planned 2027 capacity on those terms today

The AI cloud already delivered a 49.7% adjusted EBITDA margin in Q2, so this is not a theoretical 2030 margin story.

Those contract-level economics are not consistent with a mature 6% project return unless management’s disclosed payback framework is fundamentally wrong.

What the consolidated model shows is that extraordinarily attractive new cohorts can coexist with a much lower reported corporate return during the years when the company is continuously front-loading the next wave of infrastructure.

Project returns, sponsor-capital returns and consolidated accounting ROIC are not interchangeable.

Fifth, the financing structure matters because Nebius is recycling contracted assets into new growth.

The July $775M secured facility is backed by deployed GPU infrastructure and investment-grade contracted cash flows.

It is priced at SOFR + 2.50%.

Nebius stated that the financing, together with cash flows under the customer agreement, covers more than 100% of the CapEx required for the underlying GPU infrastructure.

That means an operational asset can repay or refinance the capital used to deploy it while releasing corporate capital for the next cohort.

Nebius has more than $40B of additional customer commitments against which it expects to repeat that structure.

Again, this does not make capital free.

It means gross PP&E is not the same thing as permanent sponsor capital.

The sector evidence points the same way.

$CRWV  has moved former-generation A100 GPUs into new contracts while maintaining high utilization, including an A100 contract extending into 2029.

NVIDIA has also announced financing initiatives intended to mobilize more than $500B of third-party AI-infrastructure capital.

Compute is increasingly being underwritten as a cash-flowing asset class rather than zero-residual-value equipment.

That does not make GPUs immortal.

Our Base model carries a seven-year economic life and approximately $33.1B of normalized annual replacement capital in 2030.

It does mean a two-to-three-year product cycle cannot simply be treated as a two-to-three-year economic life.

Finally, our model does not hide the capital-intensity problem.

It is built around it.

Our 2030 Base case carries:

Recognized revenue: $103.2B
Adjusted EBITDA: $56.1B
GAAP D&A: ~$40.0B
Normalized replacement capital: ~$33.1B
Normalized owner FCF before growth CapEx: $16.0B
Net debt and lease claims: $90.9B
Fully diluted shares: ~445M

We model roughly $12B of additional common equity issuance in Base and substantially more in Bear.

That is not a model pretending EBITDA equals cash flow.

The entire report is an attempt to quantify exactly how much capital the business consumes before value reaches common shareholders.

If Nebius reaches a mature, fully ramped state and earns only 6% on properly measured average net invested capital, then the bull case is wrong.

But that is not what your calculation establishes.

It takes a partial-year 2030 EBIT numerator, divides it by something close to average gross cumulative CapEx, does not consistently rebuild the denominator when the depreciation schedule changes, and does not net the customer-funded operating liabilities financing the assets.

That calculation identifies the accounting trough of a company still spending $67B a year to expand.

It does not establish that Nebius’s mature project economics or sponsor-capital returns are 6%.

text:
Q2 did not settle the $NBIS debate. It killed the easy version of it.

Revenue grew 454% year over year. AI Cloud ARR exited June at $3.0B. Adjusted EBITDA margin reached 49.7%.

Those numbers prove the business works.

They do not tell investors whether a share of NBIS ultimately captures the economics after hundreds of billions of dollars of infrastructure, GPUs, leases, replacement capital, debt and dilution move through the system.

We rebuilt our Nebius model (first comment) from the ground up to answer that question.

THE STREET’S 2027 NUMBER IS WRONG

@RealJimChanos  recently pointed to a real disconnect.

Street expects roughly $11.5B of 2027 revenue. Nebius should operate around 1.5 GW of average connected capacity that year. 

Divide one by the other and you get less than $10M of revenue per connected MW, nowhere near the $20M to $25M per MW midterm contracts or $40M to $50M short-duration contracts Nebius is now signing.

The numbers do not reconcile because the comparison uses the wrong denominator and the wrong timing convention.

Connected facility power is not billable IT power.

Year-end capacity is not average capacity.

Exit ARR is not recognized annual revenue.

New-contract ACV per MW is not fleet-wide revenue per MW.

Our 2027 Base case models roughly:

1.50 GW of average connected power
1.059 GW of average billable IT power
1.596 GW of year-end billable IT power
1.074 GW of new billable capacity at $19.87M of ARR per MW
$31.56B of AI platform exit ARR
$20.01B of recognized group revenue

That is approximately 74% above the Street number Chanos cited.

We are not trying to reconcile our work down to consensus. We think consensus is materially too low because most sell-side models still do not properly model commissioning, PUE, customer acceptance, contract cohorts and partial-year revenue recognition.

The contradiction is not inside Nebius’s contract disclosures. It is inside Street’s model.

WHAT THE BUILD ACTUALLY COSTS

Every megawatt in our forecast now traces to a named facility or sits inside an explicit undisclosed capacity bucket.

We do not assign unidentified capacity to Oklahoma, Spain, Estonia or any other geography just because the company has employees or operating signals there.

In our 2030 Base case, 4,086 MW maps to named sites. Another 2,114 MW remains undisclosed or unannounced.

That uncertainty is visible instead of being disguised as fake geographic precision.

Cost depends on the structure of each site.

Owned greenfield requires the most sponsor capital.

Build-to-suit reduces upfront cash requirements but creates lease claims.

Colocation relies more heavily on partner infrastructure.

The Base 2030 cost stack is approximately:

$18.89M of physical infrastructure cost per connected MW

$37.69M of compute, networking and storage per incremental active IT MW

$59.30M of total cash build cost per incremental active IT MW

Management has described the current capital stack as roughly 20% data-center implementation and 80% GPU deployment. Our 2026 bottom-up model lands at approximately 17.4% physical infrastructure and 82.6% compute.

The resulting cumulative Base growth CapEx from 2026 through 2030 is roughly $285B.

That is the number investors have to confront. Not because demand is weak, but because extraordinary demand still has to be physically delivered.

MARGINAL CONTRACT PRICING IS NOT FLEET PRICING

The bull-side shortcut is just as important to evaluate as the bear side. (and we address some very well formed analyses from @JonahLupton and @meeijer in the report)

You cannot take the best contract Nebius signs today and apply it to every MW operating in 2030.

Our 2027 Base cohort is composed of long-duration investment-grade contracts, core midterm contracts and short-duration scarcity capacity.

The weighted headline economics are roughly $21.6M per MW.

After realization adjustments, the cohort enters at $19.87M per billable MW.

But each cohort expires and reprices on its own schedule. The installed fleet contains different hardware generations, contract durations, customer types and renewal economics.

That is why Base realized fleet revenue reaches roughly $19.19M per average billable MW in 2030 while the newest cohort enters above $21M.

Both figures are correct. They measure different things.

Our Base operating model reaches:

2026 revenue: $3.2B
2027 revenue: $20.0B
2028 revenue: $45.9B
2029 revenue: $73.9B
2030 revenue: $103.2B

2030 adjusted EBITDA reaches approximately $56.1B at a 54.4% margin.

EBITDA IS NOT WHAT THE OWNER KEEPS

Michael Burry’s @michaeljburry  depreciation criticism gets butchered by both sides.

Accounting life, physical life, commercial life and economic productivity are not the same thing.

$CRWV  is recontracting A100 capacity into 2029 despite the architecture launching in 2020. That is strong evidence that older GPUs do not become commercially worthless after two or three years.

It does not mean an old GPU retains frontier pricing forever.

It also does not answer the power-opportunity-cost problem. A functioning accelerator can still deserve replacement if newer hardware produces several times more value from the same scarce, permitted and energized MW.

So our model separates GAAP depreciation from normalized replacement capital.

In Base:

Revenue: $103.2B
Adjusted EBITDA: $56.1B
GAAP depreciation: approximately $40.0B
Interest expense: approximately $5.0B
Normalized replacement reserve: approximately $33.1B
Normalized owner free cash flow: approximately $16.0B

In Bear, Nebius still reaches approximately $62.8B of revenue and $29.5B of adjusted EBITDA.

Normalized owner free cash flow is negative $10.3B.

That is the point.

A company can become enormous and still be a poor investment if maintaining the machine consumes more capital than the machine produces.

WHO FUNDS THE BUILD DECIDES THE STOCK OUTCOME

Our financing waterfall runs through customer prepayments, internal operating cash, secured debt, strategic-asset monetization and common equity, in that order.

Across the Base forecast, cumulative funding includes approximately:

$96.5B of customer prepayments
$98.1B of secured and project debt
$2.3B of strategic-asset monetization
$12.0B of common equity

Customer prepayments are not free money.
They may require lower pricing, longer duration, priority access or other commercial concessions. 

The exact counterfactual cost is not publicly disclosed, so we stress it rather than inventing a precise answer.

The share-count dispersion is where the model becomes violent.

2030 fully diluted shares:
Bear: approximately 686.8M
Base: approximately 445.0M
Bull: approximately 402.6M

Bear builds less infrastructure than Bull but issues dramatically more stock because weaker contract quality reduces prepayments and debt capacity exactly when capital becomes most expensive.

That is why the same business can support radically different shareholder outcomes without requiring AI demand to disappear.

HYPERSCALERS ARE A FINANCING BRIDGE, NOT THE END STATE

Arkady’s position is the right one: hyperscalers are friends today and competitors tomorrow.

The large Microsoft and Meta contracts provide cash flow, prepayments, investment-grade collateral, utilization and proof that Nebius can deliver at scale.

Nebius is using those contracts to finance the infrastructure and platform it needs to broaden beyond them.

The long-term thesis is not that Microsoft rents Nebius GPUs forever.

It is that Nebius uses today’s hyperscaler economics to build Token Factory, Aether, managed inference, open-model support, enterprise relationships and an asset-light distribution layer before those customers internalize more capacity.

The Base case includes 1.5 GW of partner-financed capacity by 2030, producing approximately $9.75B of revenue at a 70% margin.

Delivering the same revenue through owned infrastructure would require roughly 490 MW of billable IT capacity and close to $29B of additional CapEx.

That is why the asset-light model could matter so much. It is also why we refuse to value it as proven software economics before it scales.

WHAT WE PUBLISHED

The operating model is public.

The site-by-site capacity schedule, connected-to-billable conversion, build-cost engine, contract cohorts, replacement-capital logic, financing waterfall, debt treatment, dilution mechanics and principal risks are all laid out in full.

Premium members receive the Bear, Base and Bull per-share valuations, scenario probabilities, probability-weighted target, present value, required-return framework, action bands and the downloadable 38-tab workbook behind the research.

Memberships are Northwise’s only revenue source. No ads, affiliate links, sponsored coverage or paid placements.

We also launched the rebuilt Northwise site at http://northwiseproject.com.

It is no longer a chronological pile of articles. 

Research now connects through company pages, models, related theses, portfolio activity and structured filters. Premium members can access live valuation outputs and downloadable workbooks, while free accounts can follow companies, save research and receive alerts.

The core Nebius question is no longer whether AI demand exists.

It is whether the company can convert an unprecedented physical build into durable fleet economics without allowing debt, leases, replacement capital and dilution to absorb the value before it reaches common shareholders.

That is the problem our rebuilt model is designed to solve.

text:
One of the strongest bear cases against the neoclouds is being dismantled from both directions at once.

For the last year, the argument against $NBIS , $IREN  and $CRWV  has been relatively straightforward. These companies require almost unimaginable amounts of capital to build their infrastructure, while the GPUs sitting inside that infrastructure supposedly depreciate so quickly that the economics cannot justify the financing required to buy them.

We have spent months modeling this problem from the physical layer up. Across the major neoclouds we cover, our models point toward roughly $750 billion of cumulative gross buildout requirements through 2030 if these companies execute anywhere close to their stated ambitions.

That number is enormous. It is also why we have never dismissed the financing side of the bear case.

What has changed is the evidence.

$NVDA is now working with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to create dedicated AI compute financing platforms capable of mobilizing more than $500 billion of third-party capital. 

NVIDIA is explicitly arguing that compute should become an investable asset class, supported by long-duration usage, transferable workloads and residual economic value.

That is not a small development for a sector whose largest constraint may ultimately be access to capital.

We are already seeing what this looks like at the company level.

$IREN recently financed approximately 96% of the $5.81 billion of GPU CapEx behind its Microsoft deployment when its $3.65 billion investment-grade GPU financing is combined with customer prepayments. The average financing cost across that GPU CapEx is approximately 3.31%.

Nebius expects more than $9 billion of customer prepayments in 2026, has begun using asset-backed financing against deployed infrastructure and contracted cash flows, and just raised another $5 billion through convertible debt.

CoreWeave has also been progressively lowering its financing costs while opening increasingly institutional pools of infrastructure capital.

The bear argument was that hundreds of billions of dollars of AI infrastructure would eventually overwhelm these balance sheets.

Instead, the financial system is beginning to build an entirely new capital market around the assets.

That alone would be important. But something even more interesting is happening on the other side of the equation.

The depreciation argument is weakening at the same time.

The conventional assumption has been that NVIDIA's product cadence makes GPUs economically obsolete within only a few years. New architecture arrives, older chips lose pricing power, utilization falls and the collateral underneath these enormous financing facilities deteriorates.

That is not what we are seeing.

CoreWeave recently disclosed a multi-year renewal involving A100 infrastructure extending through 2029.

The A100 was introduced in 2020.

CoreWeave has also reported that pricing across A100s, H100s, H200s and L40s has been increasing, with older-generation hardware remaining heavily utilized as inference workloads absorb enormous quantities of compute.

Nebius reported something similar in Q2. Pricing on older-generation GPUs increased by more than 30% versus Q1.

Think about what that means for the depreciation debate.

The question was never whether an A100 physically turns off when Blackwell or Rubin arrives. The question was whether it could continue producing economically useful cash flow.

We are now seeing hardware approaching a decade from introduction being contracted years into the future while pricing on prior generations is still rising.

And at the exact same time that the expected economic life of the assets appears to be extending, the amount of revenue those assets can produce is being repriced dramatically higher.

Nebius' Q2 contracts averaged roughly $20 million to $25 million of annual contract value per MW.

For short-duration capacity, management discussed economics reaching approximately $40 million to $50 million per MW, sometimes higher.

Those figures should not simply be dropped into a five-year fleet model. Short-duration scarcity pricing is not the same thing as sustainable blended revenue per MW.

But investors should not ignore what the marginal pricing is telling us either.

Our previous $NBIS models were already considered extremely aggressive because we assumed revenue density could rise meaningfully as power density increased, newer GPUs improved throughput and Nebius moved further up the software stack.

The actual commercial evidence is now pushing above assumptions that were considered ridiculous only months ago.

$IREN is moving in the same direction. Its 480 MW 2026 AI Cloud target now supports more than $4 billion of targeted ARR, up from $3.7 billion without an increase in the 480 MW capacity figure. That pushes targeted annualized revenue above $8.3 million per gross MW before the broader platform is anywhere close to mature.

CoreWeave is also reporting stronger pricing across multiple GPU generations while remaining effectively sold out across much of its fleet.

This is where we think the neocloud discussion gets much more interesting.

The old bear framework effectively assumed:

Expensive capital + rapidly depreciating assets + eventual pricing compression.

What is emerging instead is:

Cheaper capital + longer economic asset lives + rising revenue density.

If that continues, the economics do not improve linearly.

The numerator, denominator and duration all move at the same time.

A megawatt producing more revenue is more valuable.

If cheaper financing requires less permanent equity to build that megawatt, existing shareholders retain more of the economics.

If the GPUs inside that megawatt continue earning for longer than expected, the period over which the original investment produces cash expands.

And we have not even reached what may ultimately be the highest-value part of the model.

The current revenue-per-MW figures remain dominated by infrastructure and compute.

Nebius is building Aether for enterprise AI workloads and Token Factory for inference. CoreWeave is pushing further into inference, orchestration and software. IREN acquired Mirantis and is moving from bare-metal capacity toward managed cloud services.

If these companies can eventually layer meaningful software, inference, orchestration and platform revenue on top of infrastructure that is already generating better-than-expected economics, revenue density has another path higher that does not require another megawatt of power.

None of this means the bear case has disappeared.

$NBIS, $IREN and $CRWV still have to execute some of the largest capital programs ever attempted by companies of their size. Pricing can normalize. Supply can catch demand. Financing markets can close. Customers can gain bargaining power. Software ambitions can fail.

But bears should be willing to update their assumptions when the evidence changes.

Right now, the evidence is changing quickly.

The cost of financing AI infrastructure is moving lower.

The assumed economic life of the GPUs is moving longer.

The revenue being generated per MW is moving higher.

And NVIDIA is actively helping build the capital markets infrastructure necessary to finance hundreds of billions of dollars of additional capacity.

For a sector expected to require roughly $750 billion of gross buildout capital through 2030, we struggle to think of a more important combination of developments.

The neocloud bear case was built around the idea that the assets would become obsolete faster than the companies could economically finance them.

So far, both sides of that equation are moving in the opposite direction.

text:
One of the stranger things happening in space right now is that $SPCX  may be strengthening part of the $RKLB thesis by becoming too successful.

The lazy bear case on Rocket Lab has always been that Falcon 9 is simply too dominant. It is cheaper on a per-kilogram basis, more proven, higher cadence, and backed by a company that has completely changed the economics of launch. 

If that is the whole framework, it is easy to stop the analysis there and decide Rocket Lab will always be a niche player living in SpaceX’s shadow.

We think that misses what is changing.

The more launch capacity SpaceX devotes to Starlink, the less relevant the theoretical total supply of Falcon 9 becomes for outside customers. At that point the question is no longer how many launches SpaceX is capable of performing. The question is how much independent launch capacity remains available after SpaceX serves its own network first.

That distinction matters.

SpaceX is not increasingly using Falcon 9 to maximize third-party launch revenue. It is increasingly using Falcon 9 to build and reinforce Starlink, which is a much larger strategic prize. That is rational on their part, but it also means the dominant launch provider is no longer a neutral merchant supplier in the way many investors still implicitly model it.

That creates room for a company like Rocket Lab in a way that simple payload math does not capture.

Rocket Lab completed its 93rd Electron mission today, its 14th Electron launch of 2026, and its ninth successful iQPS deployment. Just as importantly, iQPS still has nine additional dedicated Electron launches booked through 2030. That is not a customer treating Electron like a consolation prize because Falcon 9 is unavailable for a month. That is a customer buying into dedicated access, schedule certainty, orbital precision, and a launch partner that is aligned with its own constellation buildout.

This is where we think the market still tends to flatten Rocket Lab into the wrong category.

Rocket Lab is not trying to out-SpaceX SpaceX. It is not trying to win a commodity launch war on the exact same terms. Launch was the front door. The company has spent years building out what sits behind it: spacecraft, components, mission operations, government programs, and now potentially a much larger recurring infrastructure layer through Iridium.

That is why we think Neutron matters, but not for the reason many people frame it.

The question is not whether Neutron can simply “beat” Falcon 9. The more interesting question is what reliable independent medium-lift capacity is worth in a market where the dominant provider is increasingly consuming its own launch supply to support a vertically integrated network strategy.

Viewed through that lens, SpaceX is not just a competitor. It is also proof of the economic logic Rocket Lab is following.

SpaceX understood that the highest-value part of space was never just selling the ride. It was owning more of the stack that comes after the ride. That is what Starlink is. Rocket Lab is following the same general logic from a different starting point. It began with launch, but it is steadily moving toward a model where launch, spacecraft, networks, and recurring services reinforce one another.

That is exactly why the Iridium deal matters so much to us. If it closes, Rocket Lab is no longer merely a company that launches and builds infrastructure for other people. It becomes a company that can increasingly own the infrastructure itself, operate the network, and collect recurring economics from the services layer.

So when we look at the current space market, we do not see SpaceX dominance as automatically invalidating the Rocket Lab thesis.

We see a world where the largest player is pulling more launch capacity inward to serve its own constellation, while Rocket Lab continues to establish itself as one of the few credible independent providers of dedicated access and, over time, potentially a far more vertically integrated space infrastructure platform.

In other words, the most important consequence of SpaceX’s success may not be that it crushes every other space company.

It may be that it keeps proving why the best businesses in space eventually try to become much more than launch companies.

We published this report for Northwise members on July 25 after IREN announced $2.8 billion of new cloud contracts, raised its 2026 AI Cloud ARR target above $4 billion, disclosed that roughly 85% of that target was already under contract, and showed that customers were beginning to fund a meaningful portion of the GPU build themselves.

The model was built around a reference price near $40.60 and tried to answer a much harder question than whether AI demand would remain strong: how much of the platform IREN is building could actually belong to each existing share by 2030.

The results were some of the widest we have ever published.

Our distressed recovery case came to $22.50 per share.

Our dilutive bear case came to $14.08.

Our base case came to $214.38.

Our bull case came to $795.65.

Check out the full report and methodology in the first comment. ⤵️

After assigning a 7.5% probability to distressed recovery, 30% to the bear case, 52.5% to base and only 10% to bull, the model produced a probability-weighted 2030 value of $198.03 per share. 

At the reference price used in the report, that implied an expected annualized return of roughly 42.8%.

The important part is that the $795 bull case was never the thesis.

Our most likely outcome was the $214 base case, while more than a third of the probability distribution still sat behind outcomes of $22.50 or $14.08. 

We were modeling a company that could become enormously valuable while acknowledging that financing, dilution, hardware refresh, customer concentration and execution could still destroy much of that value before it reached shareholders.

That is exactly why we think this report is worth opening before earnings.

Since members received the model, IREN has already cleared one of the gates we explicitly said mattered. Microsoft accepted Horizon 1, the first 50 MW of the company’s 200 MW Microsoft deployment, and NVIDIA awarded the GB300 NVL72 deployment Exemplar Cloud status.

Our entire framework follows a megawatt from secured power through energization, construction, GPU installation, commissioning, customer acceptance, utilization and finally cash generation. 

Until a sophisticated customer actually accepts the infrastructure, a very large amount of apparent value is still sitting somewhere upstream of revenue.

IREN has now crossed that gate once.

Next week should give us considerably more information about the gates that remain.

We will be watching the 2026 deployment cadence, progress toward 1.2 GW in 2027, additional contracting, realized revenue density, customer prepayments, financing terms, managed cloud economics, dilution and the speed at which contracted ARR becomes accepted and revenue producing capacity.

Those variables matter because this model is extraordinarily sensitive to them. In our base case, IREN reaches 6.0 GW of physical capacity and 4.6 GW of equipped capacity by 2030. It is targeting 5 GW of contracted power by year end, has more than $40 billion of customer commitments, and is simultaneously deploying new data centers, GPUs, networking, storage and the software layer required to turn that infrastructure into a functioning AI cloud.

The more important question is how it finances the build.

In July, Nebius also completed its first $775 million asset-backed financing at SOFR + 2.5%, secured by deployed GPU infrastructure and contracted cash flows from an investment-grade customer.

That distinction matters enormously.

If Nebius had to fund our modeled $175 billion build primarily through ordinary corporate debt and repeated common equity issuance, we would have a very different view of the stock. The economics would eventually be consumed by interest expense and dilution.

If customer prepayments fall, secured financing becomes expensive, utilization weakens, revenue per MW disappoints, or Nebius increasingly needs to issue common equity to bridge the gap, the value retained by today's shareholder can deteriorate very quickly.

Conversely, if customers continue funding 50% or more of their associated infrastructure, contracts remain strong enough to support cheap asset-backed debt, and the rapidly growing operating business begins financing more of its own expansion, Nebius can build vastly more infrastructure per dollar of permanent shareholder capital.

The next debate is capital.

This week's raise is one piece of that machine becoming visible.

Those things are not mutually exclusive.

They are what attempting to build an AI hyperscaler from scratch actually looks like.

Most arguments about AI data centers are arguments about demand. Our work on Cipher Digital convinced us that is the wrong argument to be having about this company, and the reason turned out to be more uncomfortable than we expected.

Here is what Cipher does, in plain terms. It secures land and electricity, builds the buildings, and rents the finished campus to Amazon or Google for 15 years. 

It does not own the chips inside and it does not care whether the AI running on them makes money. Amazon can lose money on every workload in the building and Cipher still collects the rent, which is a genuinely good position to hold.

The complication sits in how those campuses get paid for. Cipher borrows most of the construction cost, and the lenders are entitled to be repaid before anyone else sees a dollar. T

here is also a clause in these loans letting lenders sweep up spare cash for faster repayment, so headquarters receives whatever survives that, pays its own bills out of it, and shareholders own what is left at the very end of that line.

We modeled three futures and the physical results barely differ. Cipher builds 3.8 gigawatts in our weakest case and 4.8 in our strongest, a difference of about a quarter. 

What happens to shareholders differs enormously. In our downside, the rent from every campus covers the loan payments 1.04 times, which means for every dollar owed to lenders the buildings produce $1.04, and the four cents left over is the entire cushion.

Nothing has gone wrong in that scenario. Tenants are happy, the buildings work, construction finished on time. A visitor touring the campus would see a successful company. The shareholder just would not have much to show for it.

The gap gets filled by selling new shares, which is where the story turns on itself. Selling shares when the stock is weak means selling a lot of them, and selling a lot of them keeps the stock weak, so the next round is worse than the last. 

Our downside more than doubles the share count, meaning your slice of the company shrinks while the company itself doubles in size. 

Cipher is legally permitted to issue 1 billion shares and that scenario finishes near 968 million, which turns a financing problem into a problem the board has to ask shareholders to solve.

The upside is real and worth stating with equal weight. In our strongest case, the rent arriving from finished campuses is enough to fund the remaining construction, and the company stops needing outside money in 2028 with the buildout still going. 

A business that outgrows its own funding needs before it finishes building has crossed into something durable.

Two things trip up almost everyone reading the filings. The balance sheet shows roughly $4.6 billion of cash, and $3.7 billion of that is legally committed to specific construction sites, leaving headquarters closer to $1 billion. 

And the widely quoted 5.3 gigawatt portfolio is total campus power, while rent is charged only on the portion reaching the computers, which is about 70% after cooling and electrical losses.

What Cipher has already proven is substantial. Amazon and Google do not sign 15-year commitments on optimism, and $11.4 billion of contracted rent is not a promise, it is a signed obligation. The open question is whether the company can repeat that financing across nine campuses at once, and our whole model turns on that single question.

You can be right about AI, right about the demand, right about Cipher building every gigawatt it has announced, and still be wrong about the stock. That possibility is what we think deserves more attention than it currently gets.

After Nebius’ new shareholder letter, some of the assumptions that looked hardest to believe now look a lot less extreme.

The biggest one is revenue per MW.

Our 2030 blended fleet assumptions were:

Bear: $10.8M/MW
Base: $14.5M/MW
Bull: $18.0M/MW

Nebius just said Q2 deals averaged more than $20M of annual contract value per MW.

Its four landmark Q2 deals came in at $20M to $25M per MW.

In Q3, Nebius signed a short-term capacity deal and sees pricing opportunities in the $40M to $50M per MW range.

Deal-level ACV is not the same thing as blended fleet revenue, so we are not treating those numbers as interchangeable.

But our $14.5M base and $18M bull assumptions no longer look especially aggressive when new business is already being signed above both.

Capacity is moving the same way.

Our base case assumes roughly 5.2 GW connected by 2030.

Our bull case assumes roughly 6.1 GW.

Nebius just raised its 2026 contracted power target to 5 GW and says it plans to deploy more than 1 GW per year starting in 2027.

Contracted power is not connected power. That distinction is central to our model.

Still, the physical scale needed to support our 2030 cases is becoming much easier to defend.

Financing was another major part of our thesis.

We argued that customer contracts would increasingly help finance the infrastructure required to serve them.

That is now happening.

Roughly 70% of Q2 deals included prepayments.

Those prepayments covered 50% to 60% of associated capex.

Nebius now expects more than $9B of customer prepayments in 2026.

It also raised roughly $775M through its first asset-backed financing at SOFR + 2.50%, backed by GPU infrastructure and contracted cash flows.

Management described the framework as repeatable.

This matters because Nebius does not have to fund every new MW with common equity.

Prepayments, contract-backed debt and internal cash generation can increasingly carry part of the load.

The economics are also improving faster than we expected.

Nebius says the expected payback period on Q2 deals fell to just 1 year and 10 months.

Its AI Cloud adjusted EBITDA margin reached 50% in Q2.

Our 2030 base case assumes roughly 45%.

One quarter does not prove a long-term margin, but it does make the assumption much harder to dismiss.

Demand is showing the same pattern.

TCV signed in Q2 increased nearly 4x quarter over quarter.

TCV from new customers increased more than 9x.

Pricing on older-generation GPUs increased more than 30% versus Q1.

Management says it could sell its entire 2027 capacity today on current terms and is deliberately holding some back for higher-value opportunities.

That is exactly what we wanted to see.

We said the warning signs would be weaker pricing, older GPUs losing value and new capacity coming online without buyers.

Nebius is currently reporting the opposite.

The software side is also starting to matter.

Token Factory production inference workloads increased more than 3x in Q2.

Nebius added Eigen AI and Clarifai.

Aether 3.6 shipped.

The company is pushing further into inference, orchestration and managed services instead of stopping at raw GPU capacity.

That supports the basic logic behind rising revenue per MW over time.

There are still real risks.

Nebius raised roughly $2.8B through its ATM during the first half of the year.

Dilution is real.

Capex is enormous.

Five GW contracted is not five GW built.

And $20M+ per MW on new deals does not mean the entire fleet earns that number.

Our model already accounts for a lot of this.

Base case diluted shares: roughly 339M.

Bear case diluted shares: roughly 442M.

Base case net debt: roughly $23B.

Bear case net debt: roughly $46B.

The thesis was never built on free capex or zero dilution.

It was built on Nebius turning power into capacity, capacity into contracts, contracts into financing and financing into more capacity.

That loop is now becoming visible in the actual numbers.

Our base case assumes:

5.2 GW connected by 2030
$14.5M revenue per MW
~45% AI Cloud EBITDA margin

Nebius is now targeting 5 GW contracted in 2026, signing deals above $20M per MW and reporting a 50% AI Cloud EBITDA margin.

That does not prove $1,652.

It does explain why the target exists.

The biggest question now is not whether these economics are possible.

Nebius is already showing that they are.
The question is how much of this system they can build before the economics normalize.
That is what our $458 bear, $1,652 base and $3,425 bull cases are trying to answer.

What surprised us most about this one is how little demand and differences in the capacity buildout matter for the success of shareholders.

Oracle has already signed the contracts, leased the sites, and committed the capital.

What stays open is how much of the value created by that build reaches shareholders rather than the people financing it.

The $638B backlog answers one question cleanly. Large, sophisticated customers want the capacity and have committed to it years forward, roughly 9.5 years of company-wide sales at the FY2026 run rate.

It answers nothing about delivery timing, capital required, contract margins, prepayment mix, or what survives to common equity.

Oracle generated $67.4B in FY2026 and roughly $49B of it came from software and services. Capex rose 8 times in 2 years while operating cash flow rose 71%, and free cash flow went from $11.8B positive to $23.7B negative.

The software franchise insulates Oracle from existential failure. It does not insulate existing shareholders from debt, dilution, or capital allocation.

Here is the modeling decision that shapes everything downstream.

Even our weakest scenario reaches roughly 7.4 GW of exit delivered capacity, within 15% of our strongest. Contracts exist, sites are progressing, customers are funding part of the hardware, and most capital gets committed before weaker economics become visible.

So the dispersion has to come from somewhere other than construction schedules.

In our model it comes from revenue density, margins, financing, and dilution.

Realized AI revenue per megawatt runs $13.5M in Stress to $20.5M in Bull. That produces $85.1B to $166.1B of AI revenue. Average billable capacity varies 29% across the distribution and AI revenue varies 95%.

Hardware improvement over the period is close to certain. Oracle's share of that improvement is the actual variable, and the density spread is largely a statement about bargaining power against some of the most sophisticated compute buyers alive.

A few things the sector consistently underweights.

Oracle has disclosed roughly $75B combined for customer prepayments and customer-supplied hardware without disclosing the split. Moving $10B from prepaid to customer-supplied lowers capex, depreciation, debt, and dilution while changing revenue by zero.

Gross margin cannot explain the shareholder outcome for exactly that reason.

Oracle also carries approximately $260B of uncommenced data-center lease payments, undiscounted and off balance sheet in that form. Lease-equivalent obligations in our model reach $186B by FY2029 against $155B of funded debt.

Anyone watching only the debt figure is watching the smaller number.

On capital intensity, Oracle spends $314.6B gross across 4 years against $630B of cumulative revenue, or $0.50 of capital per revenue dollar and $0.40 net of offsets. Our $CRWV model produced $1.18 on the same measure.

The gap traces directly to $19B of advance-billed, high-renewal support revenue funding a $90B annual capital program.

We also charge a normalized replacement reserve rather than whatever management chose to spend.

Apply it and Stress reports $32.0B of free cash flow but produces 21.0B. Base reports 30.5B and produces 53.0B.

The entire shortfall sits in the capital structure. Dilution accounts for roughly $3.00 and FY2030 interest of $9.1B costs about $2.13 per share after tax.

Neither requires an operating disappointment. Neither is visible in a revenue target.

Existing shareholders can still receive disappointing returns from all of it, since lenders, lessors, equipment financiers, preferred holders, and new common shareholders all get paid first.

$NBIS is building a 1.2 GW AI factory in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

We wanted to know how much of it is real, so we went through the documents Nebius does not get to write.

Our findings are in the full report in the comments ⤵️

County property records. Township ordinances. State environmental permits. Grid filings.

The grid filings do the most work, and here is why.

You cannot plug a gigawatt into the wall.

Somebody has to physically deliver that power, and long before anything gets built, the request goes to the regional grid operator.

Out there that is PJM, which runs the grid across 13 states and decides who gets connected, at what voltage, and in what year.

Those filings are public. They are engineering documents, not marketing, and the customer is usually not named in them.

On May 6, 2025, PPL brought one to PJM for a site in Gordon, Pennsylvania, a few miles from land Nebius would later close on.

It asked for high-voltage service starting May 2027.

The requested load steps up 290 MW in 2027, 300 MW in 2028, and 600 MW in 2029.

Nebius has since targeted 260 MW by October 2027 and roughly 660 MW by January 2029.

Same town, same years, nearly the same megawatts.

Nobody has confirmed the customer, so we call it strongly consistent and leave it there.

Then run the dates.

Grid request filed May 2025. Township rezoned the ground and wrote a data center framework that September. Land closed around May 2026. Nebius announced the project the same month.

The press release was the last step, not the first.

That is useful beyond this one company. Utility filings and municipal ordinances are searchable and run about a year ahead of corporate disclosure.

You can watch the paperwork instead of waiting for the announcement.

The other number that stood out was 600.

PJM's document covers roughly 600 MW. Nebius announced 1.2 GW.

Half this campus has a grid operator, a utility, and a construction schedule standing behind it. The back half has a commitment and a site plan.

That does not make it fake. It means half has been independently corroborated and half has not, and a model should treat the two differently.

The report covers the rest of it.

The land trail from a $6M county purchase to a $187.5M closing that still has unresolved acreage. The entity holding the environmental permit that nobody has connected to Nebius on paper. 

Why the campus has 30 minutes of batteries and no generation of its own. What owning this changes for a company that used to lease. And what could break the ramp.

Highridge is at 0 MW today and ramps for years.

Everything in the report examines whether or not that ramp stays on schedule.

$CRWV $IREN and $NBIS  are three different bets on AI infrastructure. 

Same theme, different risk profiles.

CoreWeave is the purest cloud growth play. 

- Over 1 GW already live, more than 3.5 GW contracted, and the most proven specialized platform. 

- You’re taking leverage risk and landlord risk. Almost everything is leased, so the balance sheet and long-term power costs sit with third parties. 

- Higher financial risk, faster revenue conversion.

IREN is the owned-power bet. 

- Roughly 5 GW secured, freehold land, own substations, 810 MW running (some transitioning to AI workloads). 

- The downside is mostly dilution and whether they can turn that power into real AI cloud margins fast enough. 

- Lower software risk, higher equity issuance risk. 

- More asset-backed, slower to re-rate on platform quality.

Nebius sits in between. 

- Best software stack of the three and owns over 75% of its capacity, with more than 3.5 GW already contracted. 

- The main risk is delivery. They still have to prove the ramp from a lower base to 800 MW–1 GW without slipping. 

- Higher execution variance than CoreWeave, more ownership upside than pure lease models.

In a portfolio, CoreWeave gives you the highest near-term growth torque with the most balance-sheet sensitivity. 

IREN gives you control of the scarce physical input and less platform risk, but you live with dilution and slower software recognition. 

Nebius is the higher-variance middle path: software depth plus ownership, paid for with construction and scale-up risk.

You’re not necessarily choosing the best company. 

You’re choosing which angle of attack in AI Infrastructure that you want to own.

$ELF recent tariff experience functions as a live case study in how pricing power, cost inflation, and consumer demand interact inside the same system. Higher tariffs increased input costs, the company responded with an August 2025 price increase, consumers absorbed part of the change through reduced volume, and by spring 2026 portions of those increases were reversed as demand sensitivity became more visible. The sequence highlights how pass through pricing exists in practice while also revealing its boundaries when affordability becomes central to the brand proposition.

The analysis requires separating effects that are often blended together in headline margins. Tariffs embedded in inventory flow through earnings as that inventory is sold, one time refunds behave as non recurring items rather than structural profit drivers, and short term freight volatility differs materially from long term sourcing shifts.
